title: Remote Work and Equity in Engineering
text:
Project Overview



Title page of the OSPE remote work and equity research project.


Client: Ontario Society of Professional Engineers (OSPE)
Project: New Barriers in Engineering and Technology Jobs: The Uneven Impact of Working-at-Home on Recent Graduates, Women, and Newcomers
My role: Research, survey analysis, interviews, report development, and presentation
Methods: Survey research, interviews, focus groups, quantitative analysis, and qualitative research
Tools: Excel
This research examined how the transition to working from home affected engineering professionals, with particular attention to the experiences of women, recent graduates, and newcomers.
The study investigated the relationship between remote work, workplace experiences, career development, and organizational practices.
It sought to identify both the benefits of flexible working arrangements and the challenges they presented for different groups of engineering professionals.

title: Remote Work and Equity in Engineering
text:
Research Approach
The research combined quantitative and qualitative evidence, including:

A survey of 1,243 engineering professionals.
Five focus groups involving 16 engineers.
Nine interviews with engineering managers and human resources professionals.

The study examined differences in the experiences of engineering professionals and explored how working arrangements affected communication, professional development, workplace relationships, and work-life balance.

title: Remote Work and Equity in Engineering
text:
My Contributions
I contributed to the research and development of the study as part of a collaborative project team.
My responsibilities included:

Supporting the development of the research methodology and survey instrument.
Conducting quantitative analysis of survey findings using Excel.
Participating in interviews and focus groups.
Analyzing quantitative and qualitative research findings.
Drafting substantial portions of the research deliverables.
Supporting the development and presentation of findings to the client.

I also contributed to the preparation and delivery of a presentation to approximately 15–20 OSPE representatives.

title: Remote Work and Equity in Engineering
text:
Findings and Outcomes
The research identified benefits associated with working from home, including improvements in work-life balance and perceived productivity.
It also identified challenges relating to communication, mentorship, informal learning, and professional development.
These findings informed recommendations concerning flexible working arrangements and the experiences of different groups within the engineering workforce.
The completed research provided OSPE with evidence to support its advocacy and engagement concerning workplace practices in the engineering profession.

title: Clean Energy Labour Forcasting Dashboard
text:
Project type: Client-facing workforce analytics and decision-support tool.
My role: Dashboard development, data transformation, analytical implementation, scenario modelling, user experience, and documentation.
Technologies: Power BI, Power Query, DAX, Excel, Power Apps
Development period: Approximately three months for initial product.
The Clean Energy Labour Forcasting Dashboard was developed to support the labour force planning efforts of a provincial government as it made substantial, long-term investments in renewable and carbon neutral electricity generation, and related infrastructure.
The project required translating an existing, manually maintained labour force model into an automated data pipeline and interactive analytical tool that made the underlying data and insights more accessible to non-technical stakeholders. End users could examine projected employment demand across 10 energy types, 3 development phases, 2 occupational groupings. It also allowed users to introduce new projects and modify existing ones through an in-application “writeback” function developed using Power Apps, and develop custom scenarios via a pop out “Scenario Sandbox” tool.
I was responsible for developing the Power BI dashboard. This included the back end data preparation pipeline, relationships, and validation, and the front end graphical design, analytical functionality, interactive elements, and scenario modelling interface.
The finished product combined workforce projections, occupational analysis, and user-defined development scenarios within a single decision-support environment.

title: Clean Energy Labour Forcasting Dashboard
text:
My Contributions
I was responsible for developing the dashboard as an analytical product, including the following components.
Data transformation and analytical modeling
Translated an existing Excel-based workforce model into a Power BI data model, using Power Query and DAX to prepare project data, implement employment calculations, and support analysis across multiple dimensions.
Dashboard development and user experience
Designed and implemented passive UI elements, including the overall graphical design, buttons, and dropdowns.
Designed and developed the interactive reporting interface, including employment visualizations, filtering, navigation, and capacity and occupational breakdowns.
Scenario-modeling functionality
Developed functionality allowing users to configure hypothetical clean-energy development scenarios and examine their implications for projected employment demand.
Project data management
Integrated Power Apps functionality to support the management of project records within the dashboard environment.
Documentation and delivery
Produced a comprehensive user guide and incorporated multiple rounds of client feedback to support the delivery and ongoing use of the finished product.
The broader project’s workforce-modeling methodology and underlying assumptions were developed collaboratively. My primary responsibilities centred on implementing the analytical model within Power BI and developing the interactive product.

title: Clean Energy Labour Forcasting Dashboard
text:
How It Works
The dashboard combines three principal components:

Project inventory: Information about clean-energy projects, including their technologies, development schedules, capacity, and development assumptions.
Workforce model: Employment assumptions and occupational distributions used to estimate workforce demand associated with the underlying projects.
Scenario modelling: User-defined development assumptions that allow users to examine potential changes in projected employment demand.

These components feed into the dashboard’s employment calculations and interactive visualizations.

title: Clean Energy Labour Forcasting Dashboard
text:
Scenario Modelling
A central feature of the dashboard is the Scenario Sandbox, which allows users to confgiure up to three hypothetical clean-energy development scarnarios by specifying project characteristics and development assumptions.
These inputs are incorporated into the dashboard’s employment calculations, allowing users to examine how additional or alternative development activity would affect projected workforce demand.
Scenario results can be explored through the same employment and occupational analysis interfaces used for the underlying project inventory.
This functionality extends the dashboard beyond static reporting by allowing users to examine the workforce implications of different development assumptions.

title: Clean Energy Labour Forcasting Dashboard
text:
Technical Approach



Diagram showing the process of calculating the the employment outputs of the dashboard.


The dashboard required translating an existing workforce model into an interactive Power BI environment while maintaining consistent calculations across multiple analytical dimensions.
Three aspects of the implementation were particularly important.

1. Employment calculations
Developed DAX measures to calculate employment demand across different energy technologies and project development phases.
The measures incorporate the relevant workforce assumptions while supporting filtering and aggregation across the dashboard’s analytical dimensions.


2. Occupational analysis
Implemented occupational distributions that allow projected employment demand to be examined at different levels of occupational detail.
This provides users with both an overall view of workforce requirements and more detailed information about the types of workers associated with projected development activity.


3. Integration of scenario results
Developed scenario calculations that incorporate user-defined development assumptions into the dashboard’s employment analysis.
The resulting employment estimates can be examined alongside the underlying project inventory, allowing users to compare baseline and hypothetical workforce demand within a consistent analytical framework.

title: Clean Energy Labour Forcasting Dashboard
text:
Delivery and Outcomes
The dashboard was developed over approximately three months, with responsibility for its technical implementation, interface development, testing, and iterative refinement.
Following multiple rounds of client feedback, the finished product was delivered with a comprehensive user guide covering its functionality and use.
The client provided positive feedback on the completed dashboard, and the project subsequently entered an ongoing maintenance arrangement.
The finished product provides a consolidated environment for examining projected clean-energy workforce demand and exploring how alternative development scenarios could affect future occupational requirements.

title: Flexible Work Arrangements in Engineering
text:
Project Overview



Title page of the OSPE remote work and equity research project.


Client: Ontario Society of Professional Engineers (OSPE)
Project: Finding the Right Balance: An Evidence-Based Examination of Flexible Work Arrangements
My role: Research design, project coordination, quantitative and qualitative analysis, report development, and client presentation
Methods: Survey research, interviews, literature review, quantitative analysis, and qualitative research
Tools: Excel
This research investigated the implications of flexible and hybrid working arrangements for engineering professionals and their employers.
The study examined how different working arrangements affected employee experience, professional development, workplace relationships, and organizational practices.
Particular attention was given to the experiences of women in engineering and the implications of flexible work for recruitment, retention, and workplace equity.
The objective was to develop an evidence-based understanding of the benefits and challenges of flexible work and identify practices that could better support both employees and organizations.

title: Flexible Work Arrangements in Engineering
text:
Research Approach
The research combined several sources of evidence:

A survey of OSPE members, with 1,199 valid responses.
Interviews with 15 engineering employers and recruiters.
An employer survey examining organizational experiences with flexible work.
A literature review and environmental scan.
Comparisons with previous research on working arrangements in the engineering profession.

The analysis examined employee experiences, employer perspectives, and differences in the implications of flexible work across organizational and workforce contexts.

title: Flexible Work Arrangements in Engineering
text:
My Contributions
I served as the primary author and day-to-day research lead.
My responsibilities included:

Developing the research approach and supporting survey design.
Coordinating research activities and client meetings.
Conducting quantitative survey analysis using Excel.
Analyzing interview findings and employer survey results.
Integrating findings from multiple sources into a coherent research narrative.
Developing the principal research reports and supporting deliverables.
Preparing and delivering a presentation of the research findings.
Incorporating client feedback and coordinating revisions.

The project involved the preparation of a comprehensive primary research report, supporting analyses, and a presentation for approximately 15–20 OSPE representatives.

title: Flexible Work Arrangements in Engineering
text:
Findings and Outcomes
The research identified benefits associated with flexible work, including improved employee satisfaction and potential advantages for recruitment and retention.
It also identified challenges associated with remote work, particularly where organizational practices did not adequately support communication, collaboration, mentorship, and professional development.
The findings informed recommendations concerning the design and implementation of hybrid working arrangements, including the importance of deliberate coordination between remote and in-person work.
The completed research provided an evidence base for OSPE’s engagement and advocacy concerning flexible working arrangements in the engineering profession.
